entries.question: 2. If K = {a, b, d, e, f}, L = {b, c, d, g} and M = {a, b, c, d, h}, then find the following: (i) K ∪ (L ∩ M) (ii) K ∩ (L ∪ M) (iii) (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M) (iv) (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M) and verify distributive laws. [Part (i): K ∪ (L ∩ M)]
steps: Write K = {a, b, d, e, f}, L = {b, c, d, g}, and M = {a, b, c, d, h}.
First identify the members shared by L and M: L ∩ M = {b, c, d}.
Take the union with K, keeping every distinct member: K ∪ (L ∩ M) = {a, b, c, d, e, f}.
This is the left-hand side of the union-over-intersection distributive law.
Compare this set with the result in Part (iii).
entries.answer: K ∪ (L ∩ M) = {a, b, c, d, e, f}.

entries.question: 2. If K = {a, b, d, e, f}, L = {b, c, d, g} and M = {a, b, c, d, h}, then find the following: (i) K ∪ (L ∩ M) (ii) K ∩ (L ∪ M) (iii) (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M) (iv) (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M) and verify distributive laws. [Part (ii): K ∩ (L ∪ M)]
steps: Write the three given sets K, L, and M.
First find L ∪ M = {a, b, c, d, g, h}.
Select members common to K and this union: K ∩ (L ∪ M) = {a, b, d}.
This is the left-hand side of the intersection-over-union distributive law.
Compare with Part (iv) to verify equality.

entries.question: 2. If K = {a, b, d, e, f}, L = {b, c, d, g} and M = {a, b, c, d, h}, then find the following: (i) K ∪ (L ∩ M) (ii) K ∩ (L ∪ M) (iii) (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M) (iv) (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M) and verify distributive laws. [Part (iii): (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M)]
steps: Find K ∪ L = {a, b, c, d, e, f, g}.
Find K ∪ M = {a, b, c, d, e, f, h}.
Their common members form (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M) = {a, b, c, d, e, f}.
This matches K ∪ (L ∩ M) from Part (i).
Therefore K ∪ (L ∩ M) = (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M), as required.

entries.question: 2. If K = {a, b, d, e, f}, L = {b, c, d, g} and M = {a, b, c, d, h}, then find the following: (i) K ∪ (L ∩ M) (ii) K ∩ (L ∪ M) (iii) (K ∪ L) ∩ (K ∪ M) (iv) (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M) and verify distributive laws. [Part (iv): (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M)]
steps: Find K ∩ L = {b, d}.
Find K ∩ M = {a, b, d}.
Combine the distinct members: (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M) = {a, b, d}.
This matches K ∩ (L ∪ M) from Part (ii).
Therefore K ∩ (L ∪ M) = (K ∩ L) ∪ (K ∩ M), verifying the second distributive law.

entries.question: 6. If A = {x : x = 6n, n ∈ W and n < 6}, B = {x : x = 2n, n ∈ N and 2 < n ≤ 9} and C = {x : x = 3n, n ∈ N and 4 ≤ n < 10}, then show that A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C).
steps: Whole numbers n from 0 through 5 give A = {0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30}.
Natural numbers n from 3 through 9 give B = {6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18}.
Natural numbers n from 4 through 9 give C = {12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27}.
Find B ∩ C = {12, 18}. Therefore A − (B ∩ C) = {0, 6, 24, 30}.
The union (A − B) ∪ (A − C) = {0, 6, 24, 30}; both sides are equal.
